title: Who is strong? (Avot 4:1)
hookLine: Ben Zoma: the strong master their impulses; the honored honor others

cards: Somebody cuts you off in traffic. Your hands tighten on the wheel. The horn is right there.

So is a gesture, and a whole paragraph of words you'd never say in front of your grandmother. And then, sometimes, something else happens. You breathe out, let it go, and the car ahead just becomes a car again.
Nobody sees it. Nobody gives you a medal. But Ben Zoma has a name for what just happened.

teach.b: Ben Zoma's third question: who is strong? The Hebrew word is gibor, the word for a warrior, a hero.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO CONQUERS HIS URGE.
teach.b: His answer: the one who conquers his own inclination. The urge, the impulse, the thing that wants to explode or grab or get even.

teach.h: SLOW TO ANGER, BETTER THAN MIGHTY.
teach.b: Then a verse from Proverbs, which in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation reads: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city."
Conquering a city is a king's glory. Ruling your own temper is greater. The battlefield Ben Zoma cares about is inside you.
Then the fourth question: who is honored? You'd think the one everyone bows to. Ben Zoma says: the one who honors others.

The verse he brings is about God: those who honor Me, I will honor. Some commentators notice that Ben Zoma applies it to people, and explain that honoring people made in God's image is a way of honoring God.
There's a practical truth in it too. Honor you demand is fragile. Honor you give away tends to come back.
So the four questions flip the world: the wise learn, the strong hold back, the rich are content, and the honored give honor.

And that ends a week of sayings: return it in good shape, not rote, know before whom you toil, start with the thing that matters most, don't finish, don't quit, learn from everyone, and today, strong is self-mastered.

how: Jewish ethics describes the lifelong work of mastering the yetzer hara, the selfish inclination, and Ben Zoma's answer is a common text for that work.

o: a priest, the man who serves at the altar in the Temple
a merchant, the man who grows rich through clever trade
a warrior or hero; for Ben Zoma, one who masters himself

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: Ben Zoma says the strong win their battles
the strong conquer their own inclination, their inner battle.
Proverbs says ruling your spirit beats taking a city
he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
Ben Zoma says the honored are those others bow to
the honored are those who honor others.

games.q: someone cuts you off in traffic and your hand is on the horn. what would Ben Zoma call strong?
o: lean on the horn. they need to learn.
breathe out and let it go.
follow them and make a point.
games.why: who is strong? the one who conquers his own inclination. slow to anger is better than the mighty.

practice: Think of a situation where your temper usually wins: a certain person, a certain tone of voice, a certain kind of mess in the kitchen.

Picture it starting and feel the heat rise; then, in your imagination, pause for one slow breath out and let the heat pass through you without doing anything. That pause is the strength, so rehearse it a few times.

wordCard.voice: Gibor. The Hebrew word for a warrior, a hero. Ben Zoma's answer to who is strong: the one who conquers his own inclination. And who is honored? The one who honors others.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: who is strong? gibor is the word for a warrior.
